summary: Describes an email authentication method, compatible with RFC 8601, that looks up the sender's IP address in a DNS whitelist. It exists to document the method in case it is seen in practice, suggest a useful practice, and register the relevant keywords. It does not consider blacklists. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Some mail servers keep a public list of trusted senders and check it before accepting mail. This document describes how a mail system records the result of that check in message headers.

questions: how are dns whitelist results recorded in email headers
what does a dnswl pass result mean
how does dnswl help with spf failures
subtitle: Recording whether a sender's IP address is on a trusted whitelist.

tldr.problem: Mail servers can check IP addresses against DNS whitelists to identify trusted senders, but there was no standard way to record and share the result of that check.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines an email authentication method compatible with RFC 8601 that records DNSWL lookup results in message headers, including which whitelist was queried, what data was returned, and whether DNSSEC validated it.
tldr.outcome: Mail systems can now consistently document whitelist results, allowing downstream mail filters to make better decisions about message handling based on sender trustworthiness.

today: RFC 8904 is an Informational document that documents the DNSWL email authentication method. It registers the method and its properties with IANA so that mail systems can consistently record and interpret whitelist lookups in message headers.

sections.title: DNS Whitelists and Email Authentication
sections.content:
DNS Whitelists (DNSWLs) are public lists of trusted mail server IP addresses maintained in DNS format. A mail server can look up its peer's IP address in a DNSWL to learn whether that IP is whitelisted as trustworthy. This check happens very early in the SMTP transaction, as soon as the connection is accepted, and can counterweight policies like SPF (Sender Policy Framework) that may reject legitimate forwarded mail.

The result can be used at different stages: early in the SMTP process to override a rejection, or later by mail filters that need to assess the sender's trustworthiness. This RFC documents how the result of a DNSWL check is recorded in the Authentication-Results header field (RFC 8601) so that downstream systems can act on that information.
sections.eli5: Mail servers can ask a trusted list on the internet whether the computer sending mail is good or bad. This document shows how to write down the answer so that other mail systems that see the message later know what the check found.

sections.title: How DNSWL Lookups Work
sections.content:
A DNSWL lookup returns one of four possible results: pass means the query successfully found applicable records and the sender is whitelisted; none means the query worked but found no A record or returned NXDOMAIN, so the sender is not whitelisted; temperror means a transient DNS error occurred (such as SERVFAIL) and a later attempt might succeed; permerror means the whitelist is broken, queries are over quota, or the whitelist returned a quota-exceeded signal, so human intervention is required.

The lookup is based on the remote client's IP address, either IPv4 or IPv6. The DNS query returns type A records with values in the range 127.0.0.0/8, which may be encoded with special meaning by the whitelist operator (for example, different octets may indicate different reasons for whitelisting).
sections.eli5: The mail server asks the whitelist list about the sender's IP address. The answer can be yes (the sender is trusted), no (not on the list), or maybe-later (there was a temporary problem, try again) or broken (the list has a permanent problem).

sections.title: Recording Results in Email Headers
sections.content:
The result of a DNSWL check is recorded in an Authentication-Results header field using several properties. The dns.zone property states which DNSWL was queried, providing the public query root domain. The policy.ip property contains the bit mask value received in the type A response, in dotted quad notation. Multiple entries can be listed as a quoted, comma-separated list.

The policy.txt property holds the contents of the TXT record returned by the query, if any. Different whitelist operators encode different information in TXT records; for example, a DNSWL might include the organization's domain name or a link to details about why the address is whitelisted.

The dns.sec property indicates whether DNSSEC validation was used to verify the data. It has three possible values: yes (DNSSEC validation confirms integrity), no (data is not signed), or na (not applicable or unknown).
sections.eli5: The mail server writes down which whitelist it checked, what answer came back, what extra information was included, and whether the answer was cryptographically verified. Other systems reading the header can then understand what was checked and make decisions based on that.

sections.title: Security and Trust
sections.content:
Some DNSWLs signal quota exceeded by returning a special code like 127.0.0.255. An MTA that does not understand this code might treat it as a whitelisting result, creating a false positive. Different DNSWLs handle quota signaling differently; some use DNS RCODE 5 (REFUSED).

When using DNSSEC validation, the dns.sec property should reflect the Authenticated Data (AD) bit in the DNS response. If the zone is unsigned, a security-aware resolver can verify this and set dns.sec=no. When data is downloaded in bulk and made available without DNSSEC, the application should set dns.sec=na.

Mail administrators should trust the whitelists they configure and understand the policy encoding used by each list operator. Downstream systems should not import TXT records without inspecting them first.
sections.eli5: Some lists report when they are overloaded in special ways. It is important to know when data has been cryptographically verified and when it has not. Mail systems should only trust whitelists they know are honest.
